doc.title: Eddie Alley interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Topsy's Roost, joining the union and busboy pay
summary: Playing drums to phonograph records at Topsy's Roost around 1930, studying at Golden Gate School of Music to pass the reading test, and joining the union in 1930 while working as a busboy.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: some free lessons. And then I worked in a place called Topsy’s Roost, I used to play my drums to the phonograph records, this was about ’29 or ’30, 1930; I used to play my drums with phonograph records until the band came. The people would dance. I just played my drums and put the records on and people would dance until the band came at 9:00. So the union said, “Eddie, you have to join the union to do this, you’re going to be a union musician.” So I went to the Golden Gate School of Music and studied music so I could pass the test.
What was the test like for the union?
Did they make you play like —
You had to read, had to read. Reading. That’s what that meant, reading.
So I took the test and passed, and I came back and played to the phonograph records.
And what kind of money would you make back then in 1929?
I wouldn’t get any money for playing music, I’d just get three dollars a night just for being a busboy, I just did that on the side.
Oh I see. You were a busboy.
In the twenties, about 1930, yeah, something like that, yeah ’29. So I joined the union in 1930. I was just a busboy. But I always liked music.
